events.title: Athenian siege of Syracuse
events.summary: Athens sent 134 triremes and over 5,000 hoplites against Syracuse in 415, reinforced in 413 by Demosthenes; the Spartan Gylippus and the Syracusan Hermocrates organised resistance, and the Athenian army was destroyed in the retreat to the Assinarus, with survivors sent to the quarries.
events.detail: The expedition is part of Italian history as well as Greek. Thucydides notes that some Etruscan cities, hostile to Syracuse since the raids of 453, sent three penteconters, and Etruscan troops fought in the battles of 413, at one point routing the Syracusans on the shore. Several Italiote cities refused Athens supplies; Rhegium stayed neutral; Thurii and Metapontum sent troops. Syracuse emerged as the leading Greek naval power of the West, and Hermocrates' career led, through his son-in-law Dionysius, to the 4th-century tyranny. The cost to Athens (perhaps 40,000 men including allies and rowers) helped decide the Peloponnesian War.

sides.strength: c. 200 triremes and over 40,000 men in total, 415-413
sides.losses: almost entire force killed or enslaved

battle.significance: Made Syracuse the dominant power of the Greek West; Etruscan contingents fought on the Athenian side.

events.title: Velthur Spurinna's Sicilian expedition (Elogia Tarquiniensia)
events.summary: Latin honorific inscriptions set up in the 1st century AD at Tarquinii by the Spurinnae recall an ancestor, Velthur Spurinna, who as praetor led an army to Sicily, 'the first of all Etruscans to cross the sea with an army'; most scholars link this to the Athenian siege of Syracuse.
events.detail: The Elogia Tarquiniensia, found in 1948 in the temple area of the Ara della Regina and published by Torelli (1975), also commemorate Aulus Spurinna, who deposed a king of Caere and fought Arretium and the Latins. They are rare Etruscan family memory surviving into Roman times, and show a Tarquinian aristocracy acting in Mediterranean wars, confirming Thucydides' note on Etruscan contingents at Syracuse.
events.debate: Identification of the Sicilian expedition with 414-413 is likely but unproven; some date it to the 5th-century raids of Syracuse instead.

events.title: Plague and famine of 412-411
events.summary: A plague in 412 left the fields untilled and in 411 Rome faced famine; envoys bought grain in Etruria, while the Samnites now holding Cumae refused to sell and Sicilian rulers sent aid.
events.detail: Livy's detail that Cumae had become hostile reflects the Oscan conquest of 421. Repeated famines show the narrow agricultural base of 5th-century Rome.

events.title: Lucanians capture Poseidonia
events.summary: Around 410 Oscan-speaking Lucanians took the Greek city of Poseidonia; Aristoxenus wrote that its citizens became barbarians, keeping only one Greek festival at which they gathered to lament their lost language and customs.
events.detail: Archaeology shows continuity: the temples stayed in use, Oscan names appear in inscriptions, and the painted tombs show Lucanian warriors with Samnite-style belts and crested helmets. Alexander of Epirus briefly recaptured the city (c. 332). Rome founded the Latin colony of Paestum there in 273.

events.title: First plebeian quaestors
events.summary: In the first election after the quaestorship was opened to plebeians in 421, three of the four places went to plebeians, Q. Silius, P. Aelius and P. Pupius; patricians reacted by obstructing the elections of the following year.
events.detail: Livy presents this as the plebs' first success in winning a regular office of the whole people. The quaestorship later became the entry point to the Senate.

events.title: Carthage destroys Selinus
events.summary: Answering an appeal from Segesta, Hannibal son of Gisco, grandson of the Hamilcar killed at Himera, landed with a huge army, battered Selinus with siege towers and rams and took it after nine days, killing some 16,000 and enslaving 5,000.
events.detail: Diodorus gives the Carthaginian army as 100,000 (Timaeus) or 200,000 (Ephorus), both inflated. Selinus had been an ally of Carthage in 480; its fall ended seventy years of peace and opened a century of Punic-Syracusan warfare. The city survived as a small Punic settlement until its final evacuation in 250; its great temples (Temple C, G) stand in ruins today.

battle.significance: Carthage's return to Sicily after 70 years; start of the great Punic-Syracusan wars.

events.title: Hannibal avenges his grandfather at Himera
events.summary: After Selinus, Hannibal stormed Himera, razed it and sacrificed 3,000 prisoners at the place where his grandfather Hamilcar had died in 480; in 407 Carthage founded Thermae Himeraeae nearby.
events.detail: A Syracusan relief force under Diocles evacuated part of the population by sea. Excavations at Himera have found mass graves from both 480 and 409. The poet Stesichorus had been Himera's most famous son; the Roman-era town of Thermae preserved its statue until Verres stole it.

battle.significance: Erased the site of the Carthaginian defeat of 480.

events.title: Siege and sack of Acragas
events.summary: Hannibal and Himilco besieged Acragas, the richest city of Sicily, for eight months; Hannibal died of plague in camp, Himilco sacrificed a child to Baal Hammon and cut Syracusan supply convoys, and the starving Acragantines evacuated to Gela before the city was sacked.
events.detail: Diodorus, drawing on Timaeus, dwells on Acragantine luxury: the citizen Gellias who entertained 500 horsemen at once, the 300 white horses of a wedding procession, the tombs built for racehorses and pet birds. The army included Campanian and Iberian mercenaries. Phalaris' bronze bull was carried off to Carthage, to be returned by Scipio Aemilianus in 146. The Syracusan generals' failure led to the rise of Dionysius I. Acragas was refounded by Timoleon in 338 and became a Punic base in the First Punic War.

battle.significance: Brought Carthage to the borders of Syracusan territory and triggered the tyranny of Dionysius.

events.title: Dionysius I becomes tyrant of Syracuse
events.summary: After the fall of Acragas a young clerk, Dionysius, denounced the generals in the assembly, was elected one of the new generals and then sole general with full powers (strategos autokrator), obtained a bodyguard of 600 at Leontini, and ruled Syracuse for 38 years.
events.detail: He married the daughter of Hermocrates to link himself to the dead leader's party, failed to relieve Gela (405) and crushed a revolt of the Syracusan cavalry on his return. He fortified the island of Ortygia as a citadel and later enclosed Epipolae with the longest Greek fortification circuit (c. 27 km), built the Euryalus fort, and created the first catapults (399). His tyranny became the classic model for Greek political theory, from Plato to Aristotle.

events.title: Treaty of 405 between Carthage and Dionysius
events.summary: With plague in his army, Himilco made peace: Carthage kept the Elymians and Sicans; Selinus, Acragas, Himera, Gela and Camarina became unwalled tributaries; Leontini, Messana and the Sicels were declared autonomous; and Syracuse was left subject to Dionysius.
events.detail: Diodorus' text of the treaty is one of the few Greek-Punic agreements preserved. The clause recognising Dionysius' rule gave him legitimacy, which ancient writers saw as Carthage's error. He broke the treaty in 397 by attacking Motya.

events.title: Six consular tribunes for the first time
events.summary: For the first time six military tribunes with consular power were elected in 405, the number that became standard for the colleges of the Veientine and post-Gallic years.
events.detail: The larger colleges reflect military need: several fronts (Veii, the Volsci, the Aequi) required several commanders, a strong argument for the view that the consular tribunate was a military rather than a political compromise.

events.title: Campanian mercenaries seize Entella
events.summary: Campanian mercenaries discharged after the Carthaginian war were admitted to the Elymian town of Entella, then killed its men and married their wives, keeping the city.
events.detail: The episode is the first of a sequence of Campanian mercenary seizures in Sicily and southern Italy (Aetna 403, Messana 288, Rhegium 280). Bronze tablets of the 3rd century from Entella record decrees of the Campanian-Greek community.

events.title: Censors tax bachelors
events.summary: The censors M. Furius Camillus and M. Postumius Albinus are said to have imposed a tax (aes uxorium) on men who reached old age unmarried, and to have compelled bachelors to marry the widows of men killed in the Veientine war.
events.detail: The censorship of Camillus is known from Valerius Maximus and Plutarch, not Livy, and may be invented. The idea of penalising celibacy reappears in Augustus' marriage laws.

events.title: Volunteers serve on their own horses; cavalry pay
events.summary: When a Veientine sortie burned the Roman siege works, citizens rated in the equestrian census but without a public horse volunteered to serve on their own mounts; the Senate thanked them and fixed pay for them, the first cavalry pay.
events.detail: The episode explains the later distinction between equites equo publico, who received a state horse and were enrolled in the 18 centuries, and wealthy citizens who served on their own horses. Infantry volunteers also came forward, and pay was extended to those serving beyond their obligation. It fits the general shift to a paid army during the Veientine war.

events.title: Veii elects a king and is shunned by the Etruscan league
events.summary: Tired of annual elections, the Veientes chose a king; the Etruscans resented him because, defeated in an election for the federal priesthood, he had withdrawn his performers from the sacred games, and the league resolved not to help Veii while he reigned.
events.detail: Livy's story indicates that most Etruscan cities were by then republics governed by annual magistrates (zilath), and that the league at the Fanum Voltumnae had a religious head. Veii's isolation sealed its fate in 396.

events.title: The quarrel of Sergius and Verginius and the loss of the camp
events.summary: Capenates and Faliscans attacked the Roman lines at Veii while the Veientes sallied; the consular tribune M'. Sergius refused to call for help from his personal enemy L. Verginius in the next sector, and the camp was lost; both were forced to resign early and in 401 were fined 10,000 asses each.
events.detail: Livy uses the episode to show private enmity (inimicitia) destroying public interest. The Capenates and Faliscans, Veii's only allies, were punished in the following years.

battle.significance: Setback in the siege; showed the weakness of the collegiate consular tribunate.

events.title: The Senones settle the Adriatic coast
events.summary: Polybius names the Senones as the last Gallic people to cross the Alps, settling the coastal strip from the Utens (Montone) to the Aesis (Esino) south of Ariminum, the 'ager Gallicus' from which they raided Etruria and Rome.
events.detail: Rich warrior graves at Montefortino, Filottrano and San Ginesio, with Etruscan bronzes and Greek pottery, show a Celtic elite in contact with Italy from the early 4th century. The Senones' raids peaked in 390 and the 360s-340s, and their territory was conquered by Rome in 283, becoming the first great block of ager publicus distributed by Flaminius in 232.
events.locName: Ager Gallicus, between the Utens and the Aesis

events.title: The Chimera of Arezzo
events.summary: A large bronze chimera, made around 400-380 and inscribed 'tinścvil' (gift to Tinia), was discovered at Arezzo in 1553 and is the masterpiece of Etruscan bronze casting.
events.detail: It was probably one figure from a group with Bellerophon, dedicated in a sanctuary. Cosimo I de' Medici acquired it, and Benvenuto Cellini restored parts; the serpent tail is an 18th-century replacement. Arretium was later a key Roman ally and producer of fine red pottery (terra sigillata).
scholarship: M. Cristofani, I bronzi degli Etruschi (1985)

events.title: The Mars of Todi
events.summary: A life-size bronze warrior of c. 400, found at Todi in 1835 and now in the Vatican, carries an inscription in Umbrian written in Etruscan script recording that Ahal Trutitis, a man with a Celtic name, gave it as a gift.
events.detail: The statue embodies the mixed world of the central Apennines around 400: Umbrian language, Etruscan craftsmanship and script, Greek style, and a Celtic dedicant, perhaps a mercenary.

events.title: Himilco's siege of Syracuse and its collapse
events.summary: In revenge for Motya, Himilco destroyed Messana and besieged Syracuse by land and sea, but plague broke out in his camp in the marshes; Dionysius attacked by land and sea and burned the fleet, and Himilco bribed him with 300 talents to escape with the Carthaginian citizens, abandoning his mercenaries.
events.detail: The Carthaginians had pillaged the temple of Demeter and Kore in the suburb, which Greeks blamed for the plague. Himilco killed himself on return to Carthage; the Libyans revolted. Carthage atoned by introducing the cult of Demeter and Kore with Greek priests, a notable religious borrowing.

sides.losses: fleet burned, army destroyed by plague

battle.significance: Saved Syracuse and established Dionysius as master of eastern Sicily.

events.title: Gauls destroy Etruscan Melpum
events.summary: Cornelius Nepos, quoted by Pliny, said that Melpum, a city 'outstanding in wealth' in the Po valley, was destroyed by the Insubres, Boii and Senones on the same day that Camillus took Veii.
events.detail: The synchronism is literary, but it marks the collapse of Etruscan power north of the Apennines under Celtic pressure in the early 4th century. Felsina (Bologna), Marzabotto and Spina followed over the next generations. Within six years Senonian Gauls reached Clusium and Rome.

battle.significance: Marks the end of Etruscan rule in Lombardy.

events.debate: Location unknown (near Milan has been suggested); the same-day synchronism is suspect.

events.title: Camillus restores the temple of Mater Matuta
events.summary: Before the assault on Veii the dictator Camillus vowed to restore the temple of Mater Matuta, founded by Servius Tullius, and to build one for Juno Regina; he dedicated the restored Mater Matuta after the victory.
events.detail: The Sant'Omobono site in the Forum Boarium has twin temples identified as those of Fortuna and Mater Matuta, with an archaic phase of the 6th century and a rebuilding on a large platform datable to the 4th century, plausibly linked to Camillus. Mater Matuta was also worshipped at Satricum, where the Lapis Satricanus was found.

events.title: Capena sues for peace
events.summary: After two years of devastation of their fields, the Capenates, Veii's allies, surrendered and received peace; their territory, including the great sanctuary of Feronia (Lucus Feroniae), came under Roman control.
events.detail: Lucus Feroniae was a major market and freedmen's cult centre on the Tiber; Hannibal plundered it in 211. The region formed part of the new tribes of 387.

events.title: Colony at Circeii
events.summary: Diodorus records a colony sent to Circeii in 393, a promontory town on the Volscian coast first claimed by Tarquinius Superbus; it was named in the Carthage treaty of 509 as a city subject to Rome.
events.detail: Circeii's polygonal walls survive. It revolted with the Volsci in the 380s and was one of the Latin colonies in Rome's later network. The Monte Circeo promontory was reputed to be the home of Circe.

events.title: No more replacement censors
events.summary: When the censor C. Julius died in office and M. Cornelius was chosen to replace him, Rome was captured by the Gauls within the lustrum; thereafter a censor whose colleague died had to resign, and no suffect censor was ever appointed again.
events.detail: The rule is an example of Roman religious reasoning from precedent: a replacement was deemed ill-omened. It was observed throughout the Republic.

events.title: Italiote League against Dionysius and the Lucanians
events.summary: Threatened by Dionysius I from the south and the Lucanians from the north, the Greek cities of Italy formed an alliance with a common council, pledging that any city that failed to help a member attacked by the Lucanians would have its generals executed.
events.detail: The league, initially led by Croton, was soon tested: in 389 the Thurians were crushed by the Lucanians at Laus, and in the same year Dionysius defeated the league at the Elleporus. Leadership later passed to Tarentum and the meeting place to Heraclea.

events.title: Census before the Gallic sack: 152,573 free persons
events.summary: Pliny reports that at the time Rome paid the Gauls their ransom, a census had counted 152,573 free persons.
events.detail: Pliny cites it to show how little gold Rome possessed then (the ransom was 1,000 pounds). The figure may refer to the lustrum of 392 or 393.

events.title: War with Volsinii and Salpinum; twenty-year truce
events.summary: Volsinii and Salpinum raided Roman territory during a famine in 392; in 391 the Romans routed them, taking 8,000 prisoners, and granted a twenty-year truce on condition that they return the booty and pay the Roman army for a year.
events.detail: This is Rome's first recorded conflict with Volsinii, the leading city of the Etruscan league, which Rome destroyed in 264.

events.title: Exile of Camillus
events.summary: Accused by the tribune L. Apuleius over the distribution of the Veientine booty, Camillus went into exile at Ardea, praying that the ungrateful city might soon need him; he was condemned in absence to a fine of 15,000 asses.
events.detail: Plutarch adds that the charge concerned bronze doors from Veii, and that Camillus had lost a son just before. The exile sets up the legend of his recall as dictator to save Rome from the Gauls. Livy also records that Camillus had antagonised the plebs by triumphing with white horses like Jupiter and by insisting on a tithe of the booty for Apollo at Delphi, which forced soldiers to return plunder. The exile-and-return pattern, with Coriolanus as its negative counterpart, shaped Camillus as a 'second founder'.
events.debate: The whole Camillus saga is heavily embellished; some scholars think the exile was invented to keep him out of the disaster of 390.

events.title: The voice of Aius Locutius
events.summary: The plebeian M. Caedicius reported that in the silence of night on the Nova Via, above the shrine of Vesta, a voice louder than human had warned that the Gauls were coming; he was ignored because of his low rank, and after the sack the Senate built an altar to Aius Locutius, 'the Speaker who Spoke'.
events.detail: Cicero mocked the god who spoke when he was unknown and fell silent once he had a temple. An altar with a dedication 'sei deo sei deivae' on the Palatine has been associated with the cult. The story turns an anonymous divine warning into a cult and blames the elite's contempt for a plebeian witness.

events.title: Massilia helps pay Rome's ransom
events.summary: Justin's epitome of Trogus, himself of Gallic descent, says the Massiliots declared public mourning on hearing that Rome had been taken by the Gauls and collected public and private gold and silver toward the ransom; Rome rewarded them with immunity from duties, a seat among the senators at the games and a treaty on equal terms.
events.detail: The story may be Massiliot patriotic tradition, but the friendship between Rome and Massalia was old: Rome's golden bowl for Delphi after Veii was placed in the Massiliot treasury. Massalia remained Rome's most loyal Greek ally in the West, invoking Roman help against the Ligurians and Gauls in the 2nd century and keeping its freedom until it backed Pompey against Caesar in 49.

events.title: The Gallic sack in contemporary Greek writers
events.summary: The capture of Rome was the first Roman event noticed by Greek writers: Heraclides Ponticus wrote that an army from the Hyperboreans had taken 'a Greek city called Rhome', Aristotle knew it had been taken by Celts and saved by a certain Lucius, and Pliny says Theopompus mentioned only that the city was captured by Gauls.
events.detail: Plutarch quotes Heraclides and Aristotle. These fragments are precious because they show that by the mid-4th century Rome was known in the Greek world, though only vaguely, and that the sack was a real event independent of Roman tradition. Polybius synchronised it with the Peace of Antalcidas and the siege of Rhegium (387/386), which is why the Varronian date of 390 is thought to be about four years too early.

events.title: Lucanians crush the Thurians near Laus
events.summary: A Thurian army of 14,000 foot and 1,000 horse invading Lucania was trapped in a plain near Laus and lost about 10,000 men; survivors who swam out to the fleet of Leptines, Dionysius' brother, were ransomed, and Leptines brokered a peace, for which Dionysius removed him from command.
events.detail: The disaster showed the weakness of the new Italiote League against the Oscan peoples of the interior, and Dionysius' ambiguity: he backed the Lucanians against the Italiotes. Laus itself, a Sybarite foundation, passed to the Lucanians.

battle.significance: Exposed the military weakness of the Italiote League.

events.title: Camillus recovers Sutrium in a day
events.summary: When the Etruscans seized Sutrium, a Roman ally on the edge of the Ciminian forest, Camillus arrived the same day the townspeople had surrendered and retook it, catching the Etruscans scattered and plundering.
events.detail: Livy says the city was 'twice captured on one day'. Sutrium and Nepet, 'the gates of Etruria', received Latin colonies in 383 (or 373).

battle.significance: Secured Rome's frontier towns against Etruria after the sack.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Mars outside the Porta Capena
events.summary: The temple of Mars vowed during the Gallic war was dedicated by the duumvir sacris faciundis T. Quinctius on 1 June 388 beside the road later paved as the Via Appia; it became the starting point of the cavalry parade (transvectio equitum) of 15 July.
events.detail: Armies leaving for the south assembled near this temple, and the stretch of road to it was paved in 296 by the aediles from fines. A 'lapis manalis' kept nearby was dragged into the city in times of drought.
events.locName: Via Appia, first to second milestone

events.title: Dionysius I takes Rhegium
events.summary: After razing Caulonia (389) and Hipponion (388) and giving their land to his ally Locri, Dionysius besieged Rhegium for eleven months until famine forced surrender; the general Phyton was tortured and drowned, and citizens who could not pay a mina ransom were sold.
events.detail: Rhegium had insulted Dionysius by refusing him a bride and offering the public hangman's daughter instead, according to Diodorus. With the Strait in his hands Dionysius dominated the toe of Italy, and Polybius dated the Gallic sack of Rome by this siege. Rhegium was later restored by Dionysius II as Phoebia and recovered its name.

battle.significance: Gave Dionysius control of both sides of the Strait; synchronised by Polybius with the Gallic sack of Rome.

events.title: Dionysius' Adriatic colonies
events.summary: Dionysius I extended Syracusan power into the Adriatic, founding Lissus on the Illyrian coast, helping Parian settlers establish Pharos (385/384) and Syracuse's colony at Issa, and allying with Illyrian chiefs to restore the Molossian king Alcetas in Epirus.
events.detail: The aim was control of the Adriatic trade in grain, timber, metals and horses from the Veneti, and perhaps a raid on Delphi. Strabo says Ancona was founded by Syracusans fleeing Dionysius' tyranny. These Greek settlements were the ones Rome later 'protected' against Queen Teuta in the First Illyrian War (229).

events.title: Latin colony at Setia
events.summary: Velleius dates a colony at Setia, on the Lepini hills above the Pontine plain, to the year after Sutrium, and Livy records its reinforcement in 379; the town was famous later for its wine, Augustus' favourite.
events.detail: Setia, Norba, Signia and Circeii formed a chain of fortified colonies around the Volscian Pontine plain. Setia's colonists joined the Latin revolt of 340.

events.title: Camillus and L. Furius at Satricum
events.summary: The aged Camillus, consular tribune for the sixth time, shared command against the Volsci and Praenestines with the young L. Furius Medullinus, whose rash attack nearly lost the battle; Camillus rallied the army and won, and generously chose Furius as his colleague for the next operation.
events.detail: Livy's set-piece shows ideal collegial conduct. The campaign uncovered Tusculan help to the Volsci and led to Tusculum's incorporation with Roman citizenship, the first municipium.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of the Pontine edge; led to Tusculum's incorporation.

events.title: Fabia, the lictor's rod, and the origins of the Licinian agitation
events.summary: Livy tells that the younger daughter of the patrician M. Fabius Ambustus, married to the plebeian C. Licinius Stolo, was startled when a lictor rapped at her sister's door to announce the return of her husband, a consular tribune; her sister's laughter at her ignorance hurt her, and her father helped Licinius seek the consulship for plebeians.
events.detail: Livy himself treats the story as a trivial cause for great events. It reflects the tradition that the Licinio-Sextian movement was led by wealthy plebeians allied by marriage with patrician houses, seeking office rather than social revolution.

events.title: Battles of Cabala and Cronium
events.summary: Dionysius I won a great victory at Cabala, killing the Carthaginian general Mago, but at Cronium Mago's young son Himilco destroyed his army, killing his brother Leptines and some 14,000 men; peace fixed the frontier at the river Halycus and Dionysius paid 1,000 talents.
events.detail: Diodorus places the war under 383-382 but modern scholars prefer c. 378-375. The Halycus (Platani) frontier, giving Carthage Selinus and part of Acragantine territory, lasted with interruptions until the First Punic War and was confirmed by Timoleon.

battle.significance: Fixed the Halycus boundary between Carthaginian and Greek Sicily.

events.debate: Dating (383/2 in Diodorus, c. 378-375 by most moderns) and sites of both battles disputed.

events.title: Temple of Juno Lucina on the Esquiline
events.summary: Pliny records that the temple of Juno Lucina, goddess of childbirth, was built in the 379th year of the city (375 BC) in a grove on the Esquiline, and that a lotus tree there was older than the temple.
events.detail: Women celebrated the Matronalia there on 1 March. The date falls in the five-year 'anarchy' of the Fasti, a reminder that the annalistic gap is a chronological artefact and that the city continued its religious life.

events.title: Dionysius allies with the Gauls and sends Celtic mercenaries to Greece
events.summary: Justin says the Gauls who had burned Rome sent envoys to Dionysius offering alliance; Xenophon records that in 369 and 368 Dionysius sent Sparta triremes carrying Celtic and Iberian mercenaries, who impressed the Greeks with their skirmishing horsemen.
events.detail: The link suggests the Gallic bands in central Italy after 390 were partly mercenary companies moving south toward Apulia and Syracusan service. Gallic raids of the 360s-340s into Latium may relate to this traffic.

events.title: Death of Dionysius I
events.summary: Dionysius I died in 367 after 38 years in power, soon after his tragedy 'The Ransom of Hector' won first prize at the Lenaea in Athens; one tradition says he died after a celebratory feast, another that doctors gave him a fatal sleeping draught at the request of his son and successor Dionysius II.
events.detail: He left the most powerful Greek state of the West, with a large mercenary army, a navy of several hundred ships and an empire from the Adriatic to western Sicily. Athens had honoured him with citizenship and alliance in 368. His son lacked his authority, and the tyranny unravelled through the quarrels with Dion and Plato.

events.title: Plato in Syracuse
events.summary: Invited by Dion, Plato came to Syracuse in 367 to educate the young Dionysius II as a philosopher-ruler; the experiment collapsed when Dion was exiled, and a third visit in 361 ended with Plato a virtual prisoner until Archytas of Tarentum sent a ship to fetch him.
events.detail: The Seventh Letter, whether by Plato or an early follower, is the main narrative and a classic text on intellectuals and power. Plato had visited Sicily and met Dion around 388, when the elder Dionysius is said to have had him sold as a slave at Aegina. The Syracusan episode shaped ancient views of the relationship between philosophy and tyranny, and the Pythagorean friendship of Plato and Archytas is a rare glimpse of the intellectual life of Tarentum, Rome's future rival.
events.debate: Authenticity of the Seventh Letter disputed.

events.title: Archytas governs Tarentum
events.summary: The Pythagorean mathematician Archytas was elected general of Tarentum seven times, against a law limiting the office to one year, and was said never to have been defeated; under him Tarentum led the Italiote League at the height of its prosperity.
events.detail: Archytas solved the problem of doubling the cube, wrote on harmonics, and according to Favorinus built a wooden dove that flew. His leadership coincided with Tarentum's great silver horseman coinage and its growing army of hired condottieri after his death.

events.title: Dictator appointed to drive the nail
events.summary: When the plague of 365-363 would not abate, elders recalled that a pestilence had once ended when a dictator drove a nail; L. Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus was named dictator clavi figendi causa, but he tried to use the office to raise an army and was forced to resign.
events.detail: Livy quotes an ancient law posted on the right side of the Capitoline temple, by the shrine of Minerva, that the 'praetor maximus' should fix a nail on the Ides of September; the antiquarian Cincius compared nails in the temple of Nortia at Volsinii used to count years. Further nail dictators followed in 331 and 313. The ritual is evidence for early year-counting and for the title 'praetor maximus'.
events.locName: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Capitol

events.title: Young Manlius forces a tribune to drop his father's prosecution
events.summary: The tribune M. Pomponius indicted the ex-dictator L. Manlius for his harsh levy and for banishing his slow-spoken son Titus to the countryside; Titus went to the tribune's house at dawn with a dagger and made him swear to drop the case.
events.detail: The people, admiring the son's piety, elected him a military tribune that year. The episode begins the legend of T. Manlius Torquatus, who in 361 won his cognomen by killing a Gallic champion and in 340 executed his own son.

events.title: Marcus Curtius leaps into the chasm
events.summary: A chasm opened in the Forum and the seers declared it would close only if Rome's greatest strength were thrown in; the young M. Curtius, saying that Rome's strength was arms and valour, rode fully armed into the gulf, which closed over him.
events.detail: Livy gives this as one of three aetiologies of the Lacus Curtius, the paved spot in the Forum: the others tied it to the Sabine Mettius Curtius in Romulus' war, or to the consul C. Curtius fencing a place struck by lightning in 445 (Varro). A marble relief of a horseman sinking into a marsh, found in the Forum, is a copy of a Republican original. The story is a form of devotio.

events.title: Military tribunes of the legions first elected
events.summary: For the first time six of the military tribunes of the legions were chosen by popular vote instead of being appointed by the commanders; young T. Manlius came second in the poll.
events.detail: Livy's notice marks the people's growing role in military appointments. By 311 a law raised the number of elected tribunes to sixteen, and by the 2nd century the 24 tribunes of the four consular legions were all elected (tribuni militum a populo).

events.title: Gauls defeated before the Colline Gate
events.summary: A Gallic war band, operating from the territory of Tibur with Tiburtine support, advanced to the Colline Gate; the dictator Q. Servilius Ahala fought them in sight of the walls, the families watching from the ramparts, and drove them back toward Tibur.
events.detail: The Fasti Triumphales record a triumph of the consul C. Poetelius over the Gauls and Tiburtines in 360. Tibur's alliance with the Gauls reflects Latin resentment of Rome after 390, which ended only in 338.

battle.significance: Ended the Gallic threat of 361-360; exposed Tibur's hostility.

events.title: Lex Poetelia against canvassing
events.summary: The tribune C. Poetelius, on the Senate's authority, carried the first statute against ambitus aimed at 'new men' who toured markets and rural gathering places to canvass.
events.detail: Livy reads it as a patrician measure to curb ambitious plebeians. It followed the toga law of 432.

events.title: Dion expels Dionysius II
events.summary: Dion, Plato's friend and Dionysius II's uncle, sailed from Zacynthus with about 800 mercenaries, landed at Carthaginian Heraclea Minoa, and entered Syracuse to popular acclaim while the tyrant was in Italy; Ortygia held out until 355, and Dion was murdered in 354 by Callippus, an Athenian of the Academy.
events.detail: Dion's rule disappointed the democrats led by Heraclides, who saw him as another tyrant. His death began a decade of civil wars and short-lived tyrannies (Callippus, Hipparinus, Nysaeus, Dionysius II restored in 346) that ended only with Timoleon. Dionysius II meanwhile ruled his mother's city of Locri in Italy.

events.title: Dionysius II tyrant of Locri
events.summary: Expelled from Syracuse, Dionysius II made his mother's city Locri his base and ruled it as tyrant for about ten years; when he returned to Syracuse in 346 the Locrians drove out his garrison and took a horrific revenge on his wife and daughters.
events.detail: Later writers (Clearchus via Athenaeus, Strabo, Aelian) told lurid stories of his debaucheries at Locri, which belong to the moralising literature on tyrants. The episode shows how dynastic marriage tied Syracuse to the Italian cities: Dionysius I had married the Locrian Doris on the same day as a Syracusan wife.

events.title: Roman revenge on Tarquinian prisoners
events.summary: In revenge for the 307 Romans sacrificed at Tarquinii in 358, Rome had 358 of the noblest Tarquinian prisoners scourged and beheaded in the Forum; the rest of the captives were killed on the battlefield.
events.detail: The numerical symmetry is suspicious, but the brutality on both sides is plausible. Etruscan tomb paintings, notably the François Tomb at Vulci with Achilles killing Trojan prisoners, show that prisoner killing had a ritual dimension in Etruria.

events.title: Forty-year truces with Tarquinii and Falerii
events.summary: After Roman armies ravaged their territory, Tarquinii and the Faliscans obtained forty-year truces, ending the war begun in 358.
events.detail: With the hundred-year truce granted to Caere in 353, the truces freed Rome to turn south to Campania in 343. Tarquinii renewed hostilities in 311.

events.title: Popillius Laenas defeats the Gauls
events.summary: With his colleague ill, the plebeian consul M. Popillius Laenas led four legions against a large Gallic force camped in Latium, was wounded in the shoulder by a javelin while leading from the front, and won; the Gauls withdrew to the Alban hills for the winter.
events.detail: Popillius triumphed, one of the first plebeian triumphs. The Gauls' wintering in the Alban hills set up the campaign of 349 with Valerius Corvus' duel.

battle.significance: Plebeian consular victory; pushed the Gauls into the hills.

events.title: The Boii take Felsina
events.summary: In the mid-4th century the Boii overran Felsina, the leading Etruscan city north of the Apennines, which Pliny calls 'chief of Etruria'; Celtic graves appear at Bologna, Marzabotto and Monte Bibele as Etruscan communities were absorbed or displaced.
events.detail: The Boii controlled the central Po plain until Rome's conquest (196-191) and the Latin colony of Bononia (189). Mixed Etrusco-Celtic graves, such as the warrior burials of Monte Bibele, show coexistence rather than wholesale extermination.

events.title: Interest halved and debts rescheduled
events.summary: Ten years after the Duilian-Menenian law capped interest at one-twelfth (8 1/3 percent a year by the usual interpretation), the rate was halved to one twenty-fourth and debts made payable in instalments over four years.
events.detail: The relief measures of 357, 352 and 347 culminated in the lex Genucia of 342 banning interest altogether, a law soon ignored. The debt cycle of the 4th century underlay the abolition of nexum in 326.
events.debate: Whether the 'uncial' rate was annual (8 1/3%) or monthly is disputed.

events.title: Valerius Corvus burns Satricum
events.summary: When Antium rebuilt Satricum and stirred up the Latins, the consul M. Valerius Corvus defeated the Volsci, stormed the town, sold 4,000 prisoners and burned it, sparing only the temple of Mater Matuta.
events.detail: The sale of prisoners as slaves begins to appear regularly in Livy in this period, reflecting Rome's growing captive labour force.

battle.significance: Destroyed a Volscian base in the Pontine plain.

events.title: Rain of stones and a festival dictator
events.summary: A rain of stones and daylight darkness led the Senate to consult the Sibylline Books, and P. Valerius Publicola was named dictator to establish a day of religious observance, with a supplication that involved not only Rome but neighbouring peoples.
events.detail: The dictatorship's range of causae (to hold elections, fix a nail, hold games, celebrate festivals) shows it developing into an all-purpose emergency office before its disappearance after 202.

events.title: Timoleon lands in Sicily and takes Syracuse
events.summary: Answering an appeal from Syracusan exiles, Corinth sent Timoleon with ten ships and about 1,200 mercenaries; he slipped past the Carthaginian fleet at Rhegium, defeated the tyrant Hicetas at Adranum, received the surrender of Dionysius II in Ortygia, and saw the Carthaginian general Mago abandon the harbour.
events.detail: Dionysius II retired to Corinth, where later anecdotes made him a schoolmaster and a fixture of the city's taverns. Timoleon razed the tyrants' citadel on Ortygia and built law courts on its site. Plutarch, using Timaeus, presents him as a man favoured by Fortune (Automatia, to whom he built a shrine); Diodorus is more matter-of-fact. The Crimissus victory (339) and the expulsion of the remaining tyrants followed.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Juno Moneta
events.summary: Vowed in 345 by the dictator L. Furius Camillus during a war with the Aurunci, the temple of Juno Moneta was dedicated on 1 June 344 on the Arx, on the site of the razed house of M. Manlius Capitolinus; the Roman mint later operated beside it, giving 'moneta' and so 'money'.
events.detail: Moneta was understood as 'the Warner' (from monere): Cicero says a voice from the temple advised expiating an earthquake with a pregnant sow, and the Suda claims Juno advised the Romans on financing the Pyrrhic war. The libri lintei, magistrate lists on linen, were kept in the temple. When the mint was set up there is debated: probably in the 3rd century, perhaps with the first Roman-struck silver of 269. The site lies beneath the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli, where remains of a tufa podium have been identified.
events.debate: Date the mint moved to the temple, and the etymology of Moneta, are debated.

events.title: Carthage congratulates Rome with a golden crown
events.summary: After Rome's victories over the Samnites at Mount Gaurus and Suessula, a Carthaginian embassy brought congratulations and a golden crown of 25 pounds for the shrine of Jupiter on the Capitol.
events.detail: The gesture belongs to the treaty relationship renewed in 348 and shows Carthage watching Rome's expansion into Campania. In the 3rd century Philinus claimed a further treaty barring Rome from Sicily and Carthage from Italy, which Polybius denied.

events.title: Loyal Campanian knights receive Roman citizenship
events.summary: Because 1,600 Campanian cavalrymen had refused to join the Latin revolt, Rome granted them citizenship and imposed on the Campanian people an annual payment to each, recorded on a bronze tablet set up in the temple of Castor at Rome.
events.detail: Livy's figure of 450 denarii per man is anachronistic, since the denarius dates from c. 211, but the bronze tablet suggests an authentic document. It shows Rome binding the Capuan aristocracy to itself against the Capuan commons, a policy that held until Capua's defection to Hannibal.

events.title: Emergence of the manipular legion
events.summary: During the 4th century the Roman army abandoned the phalanx and the round hoplite shield (clipeus) for the oblong scutum and a flexible line of maniples arranged in three ranks of hastati, principes and triarii, a change the ancients linked to the introduction of pay and to lessons learned from the Samnites.
events.detail: Livy's description of the army of 340 (15 maniples of hastati, 15 of principes, 15 ordines of triarii with rorarii and accensi) is the earliest systematic account but is confused and partly anachronistic. A Greek fragment (the Ineditum Vaticanum) and Athenaeus state that the Romans took the scutum and the throwing javelin from the Samnites; Livy dates the switch from clipeus to scutum to the introduction of pay (406). Polybius describes the mature system of the late 3rd century: 1,200 hastati, 1,200 principes and 600 triarii per legion, with 1,200 velites and 300 cavalry. The manipular order suited broken Apennine terrain and allowed relief of the fighting line, a key reason Rome could absorb defeats and keep fighting. Most scholars now see a gradual evolution c. 350-300 rather than a single reform, possibly prompted by the Gallic victories of 390.
scholarship: E. Rawson, 'The literary sources for the pre-Marian army', PBSR 39 (1971)
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
events.debate: Date, cause (Gallic defeats, Samnite influence, pay) and the reliability of Livy 8.8 are all debated.

events.title: Publilius Philo defeats the Latins on the Fenectane plains
events.summary: The plebeian consul Q. Publilius Philo routed the Latins on the Fenectane plains and triumphed, while his colleague Ti. Aemilius besieged Pedum without success.
events.detail: Publilius, returning to Rome, was named dictator and carried the leges Publiliae against patrician privilege.

events.title: The castrum of Ostia
events.summary: Roman tradition credited King Ancus Marcius with founding Ostia for its salt pans, but the earliest structure found is a rectangular fort (castrum) of about 194 by 126 m with walls of Fidenae tufa, dated by most archaeologists to the second half of the 4th century, a citizen garrison colony guarding the river mouth.
events.detail: The castrum's grid survives in the decumanus and cardo of the later city. Ostia was the base of one of the quaestores classici created in 267 and the port for Rome's grain imports; its fleet station served in the First Punic War. Excavations since the 1910s (Calza) and recent geophysics have refined the date, which some place nearer 300.
events.debate: Date of the castrum (c. 380-300) disputed; the regal foundation has no archaeological support so far.

events.title: Archidamus III of Sparta killed at Manduria
events.summary: Archidamus III, king of Sparta, called in by Tarentum against the Messapians and Lucanians, was killed with his army before Manduria, by tradition on the same day as the battle of Chaeronea; his body was never recovered for burial.
events.detail: He was the first of the Greek condottieri hired by Tarentum, followed by Alexander of Epirus, Cleonymus, Acrotatus and Pyrrhus. The Messapian walls of Manduria, with three circuits, are among the best preserved native fortifications in Italy.

battle.significance: Ended the first Spartan intervention in Italy.

events.title: Timoleon's resettlement of Greek Sicily
events.summary: After the Crimissus and peace with Carthage, Timoleon expelled or executed the remaining tyrants (Hicetas, Mamercus of Catana), invited settlers from Greece (Plutarch claims 60,000), refounded Acragas and Gela, gave Syracuse a moderate constitution, and retired, blind, to die honoured in 337/336.
events.detail: The annual priest of Zeus Olympios (amphipolos) became the eponymous official of Syracuse, a post that survived into Roman times. Archaeology shows a remarkable revival of Sicilian towns in the late 4th century: new houses and public buildings at Morgantina, Camarina, Gela and Heraclea Minoa, and a surge in coinage including the Corinthian-type Pegasus staters. The prosperity lasted until Agathocles' coup in 317.
events.locName: Syracuse and the Sicilian Greek cities

events.title: The Aurunci refound themselves at Suessa
events.summary: Attacked by the Sidicini while Rome delayed help, the Aurunci abandoned their old town and fortified Suessa, which took the name Aurunca; the Sidicini destroyed the deserted city.
events.detail: Rome punished the Sidicini by taking Cales (334). Suessa received a Latin colony in 313 after the Aurunci joined the Samnites.

events.title: Paintings of the François Tomb at Vulci
events.summary: In a chamber tomb painted around 340-310 for Vel Saties of Vulci, Achilles sacrificing Trojan prisoners faces a scene in which Macstrna frees Caile Vipinas while companions kill rival chieftains of Volsinii, Sovana and Rome, including 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach', Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome.
events.detail: Discovered in 1857 by Alessandro François, the frescoes were detached and are now in the Villa Albani-Torlonia. They are the only Etruscan visual narrative of the archaic struggles that Roman tradition remembered as the reign of Servius Tullius. The emperor Claudius, an Etruscologist, told the Senate (ILS 212) that Servius Tullius was in Etruscan called Mastarna, companion of Caelius Vibenna, who gave his name to the Caelian hill. The paintings show a Vulcian aristocracy in the age of the Roman conquest asserting its heroic past, with the sacrifice of prisoners echoing the killings of 358 and 354.
scholarship: F. Buranelli (ed.), La Tomba François di Vulci (1987)
events.debate: Date of the paintings (c. 350-300) and the historicity of the Vipinas-Mastarna story are debated.

events.title: The Ficoroni cista: 'Novios Plautios made me at Rome'
events.summary: A bronze toilet casket from a Praenestine tomb, engraved with the Argonauts at the spring of the Bebryces where Pollux has bound King Amycus, carries the Latin inscription 'Novios Plautios med Romai fecid / Dindia Macolnia fileai dedit': made at Rome by Novius Plautius, given by Dindia Macolnia to her daughter.
events.detail: Found in 1738 and named after the collector Francesco de' Ficoroni, it is in the Villa Giulia. It is one of the earliest Latin inscriptions to name a craftsman and proves that Rome had workshops of high Greek-influenced art in the later 4th century, when Praeneste was still a nominally independent ally. Its Greek model may be a painting by Cydias or Micon.

events.title: Citizen colony at Tarracina
events.summary: After the fall of Privernum, 300 Roman citizens were settled at the Volscian port of Anxur, renamed Tarracina, each receiving two iugera, to hold the coastal road between the Pontine marshes and the mountains.
events.detail: With Antium and Ostia it formed the first group of small coastal citizen colonies (coloniae maritimae), whose settlers kept full citizenship and were exempt from legionary service but bound to guard their post. The Via Appia passed through it from 312, and the great temple of Jupiter Anxur crowned the cliff above.

events.title: First coins in Rome's name: the ROMAION bronzes
events.summary: Bronze coins with a head of Apollo and a man-headed bull, of Neapolitan type but with the Greek legend ROMAION ('of the Romans'), are the earliest coins issued in Rome's name; Crawford dated them to c. 326, the year of the Neapolitan treaty.
events.detail: Struck at Neapolis for Roman use in Campania, they show that Rome first acquired coinage through its Greek ally rather than at home. They are catalogued as RRC 1/1. Some numismatists prefer a later date in the early 3rd century. Rome's own cast bronze (aes grave) and silver didrachms followed.
scholarship: Burnett, 'The coinages of Rome and Magna Graecia in the late fourth and third centuries BC', SNR 56 (1977)

events.title: Alliance with the Lucanians and Apulians
events.summary: At the outbreak of the Second Samnite War the Lucanians and Apulians, with whom Rome had had no dealings, offered alliance; the Tarentines then turned the Lucanians against Rome by sending young men who showed fake wounds as Roman atrocities.
events.detail: Rome's eastern strategy, encircling Samnium from Apulia, depended on the Apulian cities (Arpi, Teanum Apulum, Canusium). Livy's story of Tarentine deceit anticipates the hostility of 282.

events.title: War with the Vestini
events.summary: When the Vestini joined the Samnites, the consul D. Junius Brutus Scaeva ravaged their land and stormed the towns of Cutina and Cingilia, giving the booty to his soldiers.
events.detail: The campaign opened Rome's route across the Apennines toward the Adriatic. The Vestini made a treaty with Rome in 302.

battle.significance: First Roman campaign in the central Apennines.

events.title: The Samnites surrender the body of Brutulus Papius
events.summary: After a heavy defeat the Samnites blamed the war on their noble Brutulus Papius and voted to surrender him; he killed himself, and they sent his body and goods to Rome with the Roman prisoners, but Rome rejected the peace terms.
events.detail: Livy presents the rejection as Roman arrogance that the gods punished at the Caudine Forks the next year, and gives Gavius Pontius a speech appealing to divine justice. The Papii remained prominent: Papius Mutilus led the Samnites in the Social War.

events.title: Rome repudiates the Caudine peace
events.summary: On the proposal of Sp. Postumius himself, the Senate declared the Caudine agreement a personal pledge (sponsio) not binding on the people and had the fetials hand over the consuls and other guarantors, naked and bound, to the Samnites; Postumius kicked the fetial, declaring himself a Samnite so that Rome would have a just war, and Gavius Pontius refused to accept them.
events.detail: Livy distinguishes a foedus, sworn by the people through fetials, from a sponsio given by magistrates, a distinction later repeated over Mancinus at Numantia (137). Pontius' speech denounces the trick as a mockery of the gods. Modern scholars, following Cicero, Appian and the evidence of Rome's quiet in Samnium until 316, widely believe that Rome in fact kept the peace for several years, ceding Fregellae and Cales, and that the immediate revenge (recapture of Luceria, Papirius Cursor's triumph and the 'yoke returned') was invented to soften the humiliation. Either way the episode became the classic case in Roman discussions of good faith (fides) in international law.
scholarship: E. T. Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967)
events.debate: Whether the peace was repudiated at once (Livy) or kept until c. 316 (Salmon, Cornell).

events.title: Tarentum tries to dictate peace
events.summary: Tarentine envoys reached the armies in Apulia and announced that Tarentum would make war on whichever side refused to stop fighting; Papirius Cursor took the auspices, declared them favourable and attacked, dismissing the envoys.
events.detail: Livy paints the Tarentines as meddling and vain, anticipating the conflict of 282. Tarentum feared Roman expansion into Apulia, its hinterland.
